interactions.label: Mycoplasma species are intrinsically resistant to all beta-lactam antibiotics. W

params.question: Mycoplasma species are intrinsically resistant to all beta-lactam antibiotics. Which structural feature of Mycoplasma best explains this resistance?

answers.text: Presence of multiple efflux pumps that actively expel beta-lactams from the cell

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Efflux pumps are an important resistance mechanism in organisms like Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Mycoplasma's beta-lactam resistance is more fundamental — the complete absence of a cell wall means the drug's target does not exist.

answers.text: Absence of a cell wall, eliminating the target site of beta-lactam antibiotics

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Beta-lactams inhibit cell wall synthesis by binding penicillin-binding proteins. Since Mycoplasma species naturally lack a cell wall, the drug's target simply does not exist — making this resistance intrinsic and absolute.

answers.text: Production of chromosomal beta-lactamases that degrade the antibiotic before it can act

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Beta-lactamase production is an acquired enzymatic mechanism seen in many bacteria. Mycoplasma's resistance is intrinsic — it stems from the complete absence of a cell wall, not from enzymatic degradation of the drug.

answers.text: Reduced porin channels in the outer membrane that restrict drug entry into the cell

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Reduced porins contribute to resistance in Gram-negative organisms such as Pseudomonas. Mycoplasma lacks both an outer membrane and a cell wall entirely, which is the true basis of its beta-lactam resistance.

overallFeedback.feedback: Beta-lactams target cell wall synthesis via penicillin-binding proteins. Mycoplasma species have no cell wall at all, so the drug has no target — this is the definition of intrinsic resistance.
Exactly right. Intrinsic resistance is species-level and present before any antibiotic exposure — Mycoplasma's lack of a cell wall is a textbook example.

interactions.label: MRSA is resistant to ALL beta-lactam antibiotics, including cephalosporins and c

params.question: MRSA is resistant to ALL beta-lactam antibiotics, including cephalosporins and carbapenems. Which mechanism underlies this broad-spectrum beta-lactam resistance?

answers.text: Production of extended-spectrum beta-lactamases (ESBLs) that hydrolyse the beta-lactam ring

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: ESBLs are plasmid-encoded enzymes found in Gram-negative organisms like E. coli and Klebsiella, not in Staphylococcus aureus. MRSA's resistance is target-modification, not enzymatic destruction.

answers.text: Acquisition of the mecA gene encoding PBP2a, a penicillin-binding protein with low affinity for all beta-lactams

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The mecA gene produces PBP2a, an altered penicillin-binding protein that continues cell wall synthesis even when all native PBPs are inhibited by beta-lactams. This single mechanism confers resistance to the entire beta-lactam class.

answers.text: Upregulation of efflux pumps that expel beta-lactams before they can reach the target

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While efflux pumps contribute to resistance in some organisms, MRSA's hallmark resistance is target modification — specifically, the mecA-encoded PBP2a that beta-lactams cannot bind effectively.

answers.text: Thickening of the cell wall that prevents beta-lactam penetration to penicillin-binding proteins

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Cell wall thickening is associated with vancomycin-intermediate S. aureus (VISA), not MRSA. MRSA resistance is conferred by the mecA gene producing PBP2a, an alternate penicillin-binding protein with low beta-lactam affinity.

overallFeedback.feedback: MRSA carries the mecA gene, which encodes PBP2a — a modified penicillin-binding protein with low affinity for beta-lactams. This target alteration, not enzymatic destruction, is why all beta-lactams fail against MRSA.
Well done. The mecA → PBP2a mechanism is one of the most clinically significant acquired resistance mechanisms, rendering every beta-lactam ineffective against MRSA.

params.question: A common antibiotic misuse pattern in Indian hospitals is continuing empirical broad-spectrum therapy beyond 48–72 hours without reviewing culture results. According to AMSP principles, why is failure to de-escalate particularly harmful?

answers.text: Broad-spectrum antibiotics are always less effective than narrow-spectrum drugs at treating the causative pathogen

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Broad-spectrum antibiotics can be highly effective against the causative organism. The concern is not efficacy but collateral damage — their indiscriminate use when narrower agents would suffice creates unnecessary selection pressure for resistant organisms.

answers.text: Prolonged broad-spectrum exposure increases selection pressure for resistance while a culture-guided narrow-spectrum alternative would suffice

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Once culture and sensitivity data are available (typically within 48–72 hours), AMSP principles call for narrowing therapy to target the specific pathogen — reducing collateral damage to commensal flora and selection pressure for resistance.

answers.text: Culture and sensitivity results in Indian hospital laboratories are unreliable, making de-escalation unsafe

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Standardised AST methods (disk diffusion, automated MIC systems) are reliable when performed correctly. AMSP depends on robust microbiological support — the problem is that available results are often ignored, not that they are unreliable.

answers.text: De-escalation is only recommended for immunocompromised patients and should not be applied to the general hospital population

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: De-escalation is a universal AMSP principle applicable to all patients. Once the causative organism and its susceptibility pattern are known, narrowing therapy is standard practice regardless of the patient's immune status.

overallFeedback.feedback: Continuing broad-spectrum therapy when a targeted narrow-spectrum option is available wastes the opportunity to reduce selection pressure for resistance — this is a core AMSP concern in Indian hospitals where empirical therapy is often never reviewed.
Exactly. The AMSP framework ensures the right drug, right dose, right route, right duration — de-escalation after culture results is central to minimising unnecessary resistance selection.
